meaning.text: Ralston glosses oboroten as from oborotit', 'to turn', the name of a person changed into another shape by magic.
Ralston, following Afanasyev, explains volkodlak as from volk, 'wolf', and dlaka, 'a tuft of hair', and so 'a hide'.
Afanasyev calls volkodlak a compound of 'wolf' and dlaka, 'wool, fleece, tuft of hair', meaning a being covered with wolf's hair or a wolf's skin.

appearance_forms.label: Human shape, Ralston's sign under the tongue

appearance.text: A person who becomes a vlkodlak takes the shape of a wolf.
In a Polish tale of a youth bewitched by a witch, his hands turned into wolf's paws.
In the same Polish tale, his whole body bristled with shaggy hair.
A spell for a wizard who wishes to turn into a werewolf speaks of a shaggy grey wolf with a warm hide.
Among the Russian peasantry it is believed that a werewolf may be known by the bristles which grow under his tongue.
Great-Russian peasants say vovkulaki are sorcerers able to turn into bears as well as wolves.
In one Russian story a young man bewitched by an old sorceress takes the form of a black dog.
The Vlkodlak can transform himself into hens.
The Vlkodlak can transform himself into a horse.
The Vlkodlak can transform himself into a cow.
The Vlkodlak can transform himself into a dog.
The Vlkodlak can transform himself into a cat.

scene.text: A person turned into a Vlkodlak runs about the village in wolf shape and approaches human dwellings.
Sorcerers roam as wolves usually by night and take human form again by day.
In the Ukraine and White Russia the involuntary vovkulaki live in dens and roam the forests, howling like wolves.
The involuntary vovkulaki often wander near their native village.

behavior_habitat.text: According to Russian beliefs vovkulaki are of two kinds: sorcerers who take a beast's shape, or ordinary people turned into wolves by sorcery.
Sorcerers' turning into wolves is done with the devil's help, and they are in close dealings with unclean spirits.
Dealers in the black art who have turned themselves into wolves are for the most part ravenous destroyers of all that falls in their way.
People made wolves against their will seldom disgrace their human nature, attaching themselves to men and apologising with tears and pawings.
Unless driven by hunger the involuntary werewolves never slay and eat, and when they must kill a sheep they seek one from a village other than their own.
The involuntary vovkulaki keep human understanding and almost never attack village herds; only unbearable hunger drives them to seek prey.
When they see a person they look at him piteously, as if begging for help, and tears have been seen streaming from the vovkulak's eyes.
The vovkulak will not take raw meat offered to him but greedily eats a thrown piece of bread.
A person turned into a Vlkodlak casts plaintive glances at people without harming anyone.
In a Polish tale the bewitched youth's cattle fled from him in terror, and his voice had become a mere howl.
A man turned into a wolf by a witch said afterwards that he made friends with a real wolf and hunted with him, never forgetting he was a man though he had lost articulate speech.
At night the Vlkodlak attacks cattle, sucks the milk of cows, mares and sheep, strangles horses, and causes cattle to die of plague.
The Vlkodlak may even assail human beings, frightening, beating and strangling them.
The Slavs in Istria believe that every family has its own Vukodlak, who tries to harm the house.
Among the Southern Slavs an old tradition, dating from the thirteenth century, tells of a Vukodlak who followed the clouds and devoured the sun or the moon, causing an eclipse.
The Serbs say vukodlaki appear chiefly in winter, from Christmas to the Day of the Ascension.
Among the Poles it is believed that oborotni turn into wolves twice a year, at Koliada and on St John's Night.
In popular tradition the Vlkodlak is frequently identified with the Vampire, and similar stories are told of both.

dealing_with_it.text: A person turned into a Vlkodlak keeps his wolf shape until the same person who enchanted him destroys the charm.
To cure an involuntary werewolf it is necessary either to strip off his hide or to remove the magic girdle or other amulet that put him in his brute state.
In one Russian story, on a wizard's advice, people heated a bath as hot as possible and scalded the bewitched dog's skin off, and it turned back into a young man of a neighbouring village.
In the Ukraine there lingers a tradition that a werewolf touched with a pitchfork or a flail at once resumes his human form.
Buslaev notes that a buried werewolf or vampire has to be pierced with an aspen stake.
In Russia it is thought that a sorcerer who knows a person's name can make him an oboroten at will, so the baptismal name must be hidden and another, invented name used.
Among the Southern Slavs, during an eclipse attributed to the Vukodlak, drums were beaten, bells rung and guns fired to drive the demon away.
In Istria each house also has a good genius, the Krsnik, who protects it from the Vukodlak and battles with him.

origin.text: The power of dealers in magic to transform themselves or their victims into various shapes is widely spread in Russia, and a person so changed is called oboroten.
A child born feet foremost or with teeth will become a Vlkodlak.
A person may be turned into a Vlkodlak by magic power, most often bride and bridegroom on their way to church to be married.
Great-Russian peasants say vovkulaki are sorcerers gifted with the power to turn into wolves or bears.
In the Ukraine and White Russia, people turned into beasts against their will by sorcerers and witches are called vovkulaki, because they are most often pictured as wolves.
In a Polish tradition a youth who scorned a witch's love was turned into a wolf as he swung his axe in the forest.
A White-Russian tradition tells that a hostile magician turned the bridegroom and the other men of a wedding party into wolves.
To transform a wedding party the hostile wizard is generally believed to girdle each member with a leather strap or piece of bast over which spells have been whispered.
In a Ruthenian story a witch hid her rolled-up girdle beneath the threshold of a wedding cottage, and everyone who stepped across it became a wolf.
Ralston prints a Russian spell to be spoken by a wizard who wishes to turn into a werewolf, calling on the moon to melt the bullet and blunt the knife so that none may seize the grey wolf.
The Kormchaya Kniga states that in these transformed beings the people used to see not mere mortals but 'chasers of the clouds'.

rationale.text: Afanasyev records vovkulaki among Great-Russian peasants and, as involuntary werewolves, in the Ukraine and White Russia.
Afanasyev also records the belief among the Poles and the Serbs.
Ralston's account of involuntary werewolves, with the Polish, White-Russian and Ruthenian tales and the black-dog cure, cites Afanasyev, so it is counted with him, not as a second source.
Ralston's Ukrainian pitchfork tradition also cites Afanasyev.

Ralston independently gives oboroten as the name in Russia for a person changed by magic, records the Russian peasant belief in bristles under the werewolf's tongue, and prints a werewolf spell from Sakharov.
Machal, a third author, records the Vlkodlak among the Slavs generally, with South-Slav and Istrian traditions.

names.primary.native 'оборотень' is cited from afanasyev1869:p.529, where Afanasyev prints the nominative in his own Russian prose about a Carinthian tale; the page does not attach the word to a people. Russians is assigned because Ralston (ralston1872:p.403) gives oboroten as the name used in Russia. Afanasyev's other opened pages print only inflected forms (оборотнемъ, оборотняхъ, оборотни).

Native forms on afanasyev1869:p.527 are given with abbreviations: 'малор.' (вовкулакъ, вовкунъ) and 'бѣлор.' (вавкалакъ). The vovkulak row's people Ukrainians rests on Ralston's 'Little-Russian vovkulak' (ralston1872:p.404); вовкунъ is mapped by reading 'малор.' as Little-Russian. The Belarusian form вавкалакъ is left out because 'бѣлор.' is not a table term; propose 'бѣлор.' -> Belarusians and 'малор.' -> Ukrainians.

People terms met that sources/peoples.json does not cover, left unmapped: 'Great-Russian' (ralston1872:p.404; великорусскіе afanasyev1869:p.532; propose Russians); 'Dalmatian' vakudluk (ralston1872:p.404; propose Croatians); 'Lett' wilkats (ralston1872:p.404; non-Slavic, propose no row); 'Jugo-Slavs (Southern Slavs)' (machal1918:p.229; no single people); 'Slavs in Istria' (machal1918:p.229; propose Croatians or Slovenes, contested); 'Сербы' (afanasyev1869:p.528; propose Serbs); 'У поляковъ' (afanasyev1869:p.528; propose Poles); 'На Руси' (afanasyev1869:p.549; propose Russians); 'Украйна' and 'Бѣлоруссія' (afanasyev1869:p.549; propose Ukrainians and Belarusians). Clauses keep the source words; no people rows were written for these.

Machal's own names Vlkodlak, Vrkolak and Volkun (machal1918:p.229) carry no people on the page (only 'Among the Slavs'), so they are not entered as variants. The family 'monster' rests on machal1918:p.229 (attacks cattle, strangles horses and people; called a demon); Ralston and Afanasyev frame the being as a transformed sorcerer or victim, which a reader may prefer to file as 'other'.

related: vampir from machal1918:p.229 (frequently identified with the Vampire) and ralston1872:p.406 (buried werewolf or vampire pierced with aspen); kresnik from machal1918:p.229 (the Krsnik protects the house from the Vukodlak and battles him).
Editorial: modern film and game werewolf traits (transformation at the full moon, silver bullets, the curse passed on by a bite) are excluded; this entry records only the cited folk sources.
